scope: We looked at 39 examples and kept 27 across 8 products. That is below the target of 30 to 50 because we removed unrelated marketing, graphics and setup screens. The examples show instructors managing course expectations. Course products are the main evidence. Asana is a similar idea from another kind of product, and we label it that way. The screenshots were collected earlier; we did not test the products live. If a screenshot doesn't show a feature, the product may still have it. The sections Q1 to Q6 below show every example we kept. Where two examples contrast, the difference is a design choice, not a product defect.
legend: A check mark means the screenshots clearly show that part of the question. Partial means limited or nearby support. A cross means the screenshots contradict the claim. A question mark means not shown. For Q3, a check mark can mean an explicit rule or clearly informational readiness. A missing screenshot alone never earns a cross. Asana is a similar idea from another kind of product.

top.why: Udemy has the clearest editor for course outcomes. Each outcome is a separate required item, with a character counter, and it says where learners will see them.
Kajabi links a progression rule to a specific lesson and says when an assessment counts as complete.
Asana shows a three-screen flow that links a goal to a project and makes the progress easy to see.
Udemy places a section objective directly above the content it frames, but does not link it to any competency.
Coursera makes the learner outcome list easy to review before starting the course.
Kajabi keeps generated course structure editable and gives the instructor 'Apply' and 'Discard' control.
Asana, in a different kind of product, explains each goal choice and lets people say they are not sure, instead of forcing a guess.

differences.text: Udemy treats outcomes as planning fields the instructor must fill in, with a minimum count, and says they will appear publicly. Teachable's repeated checkout bullets are optional marketing lines. Essentials should keep assessed outcomes separate from promotional summaries.

Udemy authors write prerequisite descriptions. Kajabi can lock progress until a selected lesson is done. Codecademy states what counts as complete. Skillshare shows readiness information. These solve different course-management decisions and need different labels.

Udemy places an objective within a curriculum section. Asana instead lets someone attach, search for and confirm a linked project, then shows progress. The linking steps could apply elsewhere, but finishing a project is not proof of learning.

Udemy says authored outcomes will be public, while Teachable's preview shows differences between draft and published content. A preview needs to explain what learners can currently see as well as how content is presented.

Kajabi lets instructors edit and accept or discard generated structure. Udemy limits how outcomes are entered, and Asana asks authors to define success. These controls complement each other. None of the screenshots prove AI can check whether a learning outcome is measurable.
Udemy visibly requires outcomes early in planning. Teachable's publication flow does not show that step, so a publish flow alone cannot prove that outcomes are optional.

practices.text: Use separate outcome items and say where learners will see them, near the editor. Check whether the order can be changed; these examples don't show reordering.

Give readiness guidance, progression rules and completion criteria separate names and controls. Put a concrete example in the requirement editor, and show each enforced rule's condition next to its settings.
Keep authored outcomes near the curriculum they belong to, and make later links easy to see. Treat progress summaries and assessed mastery as separate design decisions.
Pair AI assistance with editable output and a clear accept or discard action. Combine that with clear success criteria rather than assuming generated text is ready for assessment.
Offer a learner preview that makes draft versus published clear, and say plainly whether outcomes must be finished before publish.

openQuestions.text: For simulation education, which readiness items are advice, which require learner acknowledgement, and which must block an event or scenario? How would a faculty override be shown? Kajabi shows a similar rule setup; Skillshare shows the informational contrast.

Should course outcomes remain stable records with versioned wording when section objectives, scenarios or competencies change? Udemy's local objective and Asana's explicit link suggest different models. The competency and scenario sub-modules must resolve the join.

What demonstrates mastery: attendance, scenario completion, an assessment pass or faculty judgement? Codecademy's stated completion threshold and Asana's project progress are useful contrasts, not simulation assessment policy.
Must the Learner Portal keep the exact outcome wording and order, and should instructors preview drafts or only the published version? Capture one same-course round trip before choosing the contract.

At the Canvas hand-off, which system owns outcome wording, stable identifiers, publication status and assessment links? This set of examples shows local authoring and linking patterns but does not show Canvas interoperability. Resolve this in the neighbouring hand-off module.
